newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Japanese companies slow to defuse millennium bomb.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japanese companies slow to defuse millennium bomb.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technololgy Correspondent
Japanese companies are falling behind in the critical race to save their computers from the millennium bomb.

Corporations from the United States lead the way. In Europe, British and Scandinavian companies are said to be successfully cleaning up their computer software, while German and French operators, and those in southeast East Asia are lagging.
Information technology has often been the key to companies' success in the cut-throat global economy, with computers sharpening up operations in all kinds of ways.

Mundane data processing of wages and pensions has cut costs. The computerisation of record-keeping and industrial processes has allowed payrolls to be slashed, bottom lines to be fattened, and competition flattened.

But this success based on heavy investment in computers is threatening to bite back, as more companies worry that all this high technology might in fact carry a malignant virus in the form of the millennium bug.
The fear is that as clocks tick past midnight into the new millennium, computers across the world will fail to recognise the year 2000 and crash, or begin pumping out erroneous data.

Experts disagree about the fallout from this problem. Some say it is all in the fevered imagination of journalists looking for cheap headlines, or unscrupulous software companies seeking to frighten corporations into buying hugely expensive solutions they don't really need.
If the Cold War was still with us, the extent of the predicted disaster might sound like a communist plot to bring down capitalism.

As computers crash on day one of the millennium, say the doom merchants, telephone exchanges, power stations, and public utilities will grind to a halt. Banks will be unable to unlock their vaults because of faulty computer chips, and automatic tellers will cease dispensing cash. The world's financial system will reel as computers freeze in New York, Tokyo, Frankfurt and London.
State social security, health and welfare systems will cease to operate. Companies will fail as they find that over-reliance on computers means that business has disappeared into a black hole.
DISASTER SCENARIO BLAMED ON PROGRAMMERS

The cause of the problem has been blamed on computer programmers in the 1970s and 1980s who used abbreviated dates such as "97" and "89" to save precious programme space, knowing that when 2000 dawned computers would be confused by the double zero.
They believed that because of the speed of technological development, none of these systems would survive until 2000.
They have, and trouble looms.

This extreme scenario may or may not come true. But what is not in question is the fact that a theoretical problem exists, that it needs to be addessed, and some countries' big business is better prepared than others to handle it.

"U.S. readiness is about nine to 12 months ahead of the U.K., and the U.K. is about six months ahead of (mainland) Europe. The impression is that the Far East is a little way behind still," said Nick Fitzhugh, Year 2000 Teamleader at management consultants Ernst & Young.
Countries like Germany and France have been concentrating programmers on preparation for the single European currency, scheduled to start on January 1, 1999, Fitzhugh said.
Massimo Spalla, associate partner at Andersen Consulting agrees.

"Europe is some way behind the States. The U.K. is showing the most awareness in Europe, then I see the Scandinavian countries, then the others are some way behind. In all the countries there is awareness, it is just a matter of volume," Spalla said.
JAPANESE TECHNOLOGY "OUTSOURCING" ROOT OF PROBLEM
Lack of action in Japan worries some experts.

Japanese companies are said to be at a relative disadvantage in cleaning up the millennium bug because they have traditionally contracted out much information technology work. This means data processing is often out of the day-to-day management loop.

"One difficulty is that for large Japanese corporations, 70 percent of the IT budget is outsourced. The assumption is that the outsourcing company is paid to make it work," said Doug Sallen, vice-president, business development, of Dutch software firm Baan Company.
Sallen said this IT at arms-length means that Japanese companies have been slower than western companies to realise the urgency of the problem, and are more in danger of missing the deadline.
"Being late to the game doesn't mean losing, but it does make for an interesting fourth quarter," said Sallen, who is currently in Japan, selling Baan millennium solutions.
Sallen said that Japanese multi-national companies are more on top of the issue than domestically orientated ones.
U.S. MAY LEAD, BUT THIRD OF FIRMS SAID IN DANGER
But even in the U.S., many companies are in jeopardy.

"The wheels will fall off on the first day of 1999, which is a trip-wire for any companies that transact business with effective dates one year in the future," said Tom Gormley, analyst with Forrester Research, a consultancy in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
"Those without compliant packages on this date will spew out invalid transactions and data, frustrating customers and business partners, and risking significant loss of business, Gormley said.
"A third (of U.S. companies) won't make the fix in time. A late start, severe shortage of skilled resources, and a lack of prioritisation and options will be the culprits.

"A third will finish in time but pay steep costs for lost opportunities. Upgrading current applications to Y2K (Year 2000) compliant releases won't allow for desirable process changes, and most of these companies will have to run the same fire drill again for the new Euro currency.
"Only one-third of companies will make the right moves, avoiding serious losses and opportunity costs," Gormley said.
